1.1: Keep an accurate, detailed and current inventory of every enterprise asset that can store or process data, including owner, department and approval to connect.
Review and update the inventory at least every six months.
1.2: Have a process to deal with unauthorized assets: remove them, deny them network access or quarantine them.
Address unauthorized assets at least weekly.
1.3: Use an active discovery tool to find assets connected to the enterprise network.
Run active discovery at least daily.
1.4: Use DHCP logging on DHCP servers or IP address management tools to keep the asset inventory current.
Review logs and update the inventory at least weekly.
1.5: Use a passive discovery tool to identify assets connected to the network.
Review and update the inventory at least weekly.
2.1: Maintain an inventory of licensed software installed on enterprise assets. Record each entry's title, publisher, initial install/use date and business purpose. Where appropriate, add URL/app store, version, deployment method, decommission date and license count.
Review and update the software inventory at least every six months.
2.2: Reserve authorized status for supported software or mission-essential unsupported software with a documented exception, mitigating controls and accepted residual risk. Classify other unsupported software as unauthorized.
Review software support at least monthly.
2.3: Remove unauthorized software from use or document it as an approved exception.
Address unauthorized software at least monthly.
2.4: Use software-inventory tools throughout the enterprise, when possible, to automate discovery and records of installed software.
2.5: Use technical controls so only authorized software can run.
Reassess the allowlist at least every six months.
2.6: Allow only authorized libraries (such as .dll, .ocx, .so) to load into system processes.
Reassess at least every six months.
2.7: Use technical controls to allow approved scripts and block unauthorized scripts. Digital signatures and version control are example methods.
Reassess at least every six months.
3.1: Document the data-management process: sensitivity, ownership, handling, retention limits and disposal, aligned to enterprise sensitivity and retention standards.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
3.2: Keep a data inventory based on the data management process, at least for sensitive data.
Review and update the inventory at least annually.
3.3: Set data access control lists based on users' need to know, for local and remote file systems, databases and applications.
3.4: Retain data according to the documented process, with minimum and maximum retention periods.
3.5: Dispose of data securely, with methods that match the data's sensitivity.
3.6: Encrypt data on end-user devices that hold sensitive data.
3.7: Have a data classification scheme with labels such as sensitive, confidential and public.
Review and update the classification scheme at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
3.8: Document data flows, including provider flows, using the enterprise's data-management process as the basis.
Review and update documentation at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
3.11: Encrypt sensitive data at rest on servers, applications and databases.
3.12: Segment data processing and storage by sensitivity. Keep sensitive data off enterprise assets intended for lower-sensitivity data.
3.13: Use an automated tool to identify all sensitive data stored, processed or transmitted through enterprise assets, including remote-provider locations, and update the data inventory.
3.14: Log access to sensitive data, including changes and disposal.
4.1: Have a documented secure configuration process for enterprise assets and software.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
4.2: Have a documented secure configuration process for network devices.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
4.3: Lock sessions automatically after a period of inactivity.
No more than 15 minutes on general-purpose systems and 2 minutes on mobile devices.
4.4: Implement and maintain a firewall on servers where supported; virtual, operating-system and third-party firewalls are example methods.
4.5: Run and manage a host-based firewall on end-user devices, with a default-deny rule.
4.6: Manage assets and software securely. Version-controlled configuration and secure administration protocols are examples. Do not use insecure management protocols unless operationally essential.
4.7: Manage default accounts such as root and administrator: disable them or change their credentials.
4.8: Uninstall or disable services that are not needed, such as unused file-sharing or web services.
4.9: Configure trusted DNS servers on network infrastructure, for example enterprise-controlled or reputable externally accessible DNS services.
4.10: Enforce automatic lockout after a defined number of local failed sign-ins on portable end-user devices, where supported.
Allow no more than 20 failed attempts on laptops and 10 on tablets or smartphones.
4.11: Enable remote removal of enterprise data from enterprise-owned portable devices when appropriate, such as loss, theft or departure.
4.12: Keep a separate enterprise workspace on mobile devices where supported.
5.1: Keep an inventory of all accounts, with name, username, start and end dates and department.
Validate that active accounts are authorized at least quarterly.
5.2: Use unique passwords for all enterprise assets.
CIS best-practice implementation: at least 8 characters with MFA or 14 without MFA. This does not replace the platform password policy.
5.3: Delete or disable accounts that have not been used.
After 45 days of inactivity, where supported.
5.4: Limit administrator privileges to dedicated administrator accounts, not used for everyday work such as email or browsing.
5.5: Keep an inventory of service accounts with owner, review date and purpose.
Validate that service accounts are authorized at least quarterly.
5.6: Manage accounts centrally through a directory or identity service.
6.1: Follow a documented access-granting process, preferably automated, for new hires and role changes.
6.2: Follow an access-revocation process, preferably automated. Disable accounts immediately for termination, rights revocation or role change; retain audit trails when needed.
6.3: Enforce MFA on externally exposed enterprise and third-party applications where supported. Directory-service or SSO-provider enforcement can satisfy this safeguard.
6.4: Require multi-factor authentication for remote network access.
6.5: Require MFA for administrative-access accounts on all enterprise assets, where supported, including service-provider-managed assets.
6.6: Keep an inventory of authentication and authorization systems, on premises and with service providers.
Review and update the inventory at least annually.
6.7: Centralize access control through a directory service or SSO provider for enterprise assets where supported.
6.8: Define and maintain role-based access, documenting the access each role needs.
7.1: Have a documented vulnerability management process for enterprise assets.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
7.2: Have a risk-based remediation strategy documented in a remediation process.
Review the remediation process at least monthly.
7.3: Patch operating systems through automated patch management.
Run automated OS patching at least monthly.
7.4: Patch applications through automated patch management.
Run automated application patching at least monthly.
7.5: Run automated vulnerability scans of internal enterprise assets, authenticated and unauthenticated.
7.6: Run automated vulnerability scans of externally exposed enterprise assets.
7.7: Remediate detected vulnerabilities through processes and tooling, based on the remediation process.
8.1: Have a documented audit log management process covering collection, review and retention.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
8.2: Collect audit logs; enable logging across enterprise assets as defined by the process.
8.3: Make sure log storage is large enough to meet the log management process.
8.4: Use at least two synchronized time sources where supported.
8.5: Collect detailed logs on assets containing sensitive data, including event source, date, username, timestamp, source and destination addresses, and other useful investigative details.
8.6: Collect DNS query audit logs where appropriate and supported.
8.7: Collect URL request audit logs where appropriate and supported.
8.8: Collect command-line audit logs, such as PowerShell, Bash and remote administrative terminals.
8.9: Centralize audit log collection and retention as far as possible.
8.10: Retain audit logs across enterprise assets.
Keep logs for at least 90 days.
8.11: Review audit logs to detect anomalies or abnormal events that could indicate a threat.
8.12: Collect service provider logs where supported, such as authentication and data-change events.
9.1: Allow only fully supported browsers and email clients, using the latest version from the vendor.
9.2: Use DNS filtering on remote and on-premises end-user devices to block access to known malicious domains.
9.3: Enforce and update network-based URL filtering for all enterprise assets to limit access to malicious or unapproved websites.
9.4: Restrict browser and email client plugins, extensions and add-ons that are unnecessary or unauthorized.
9.5: Implement DMARC with SPF and DKIM to reduce spoofed or modified email from valid domains.
9.6: Block unnecessary file types from entering the enterprise email gateway.
9.7: Run email server anti-malware protections such as attachment scanning and sandboxing.
10.1: Deploy and maintain anti-malware software on all enterprise assets.
10.2: Update anti-malware signature files automatically on all assets.
10.3: Disable autorun and autoplay for removable media.
10.4: Scan removable media for malware automatically when it is inserted or connected.
10.5: Enable anti-exploitation features such as Data Execution Prevention and Windows Defender Exploit Guard where possible.
11.1: Have a documented data recovery process covering scope, prioritization and backup security.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
11.2: Run automated backups of in-scope enterprise assets.
Back up at least weekly, or more often based on data sensitivity.
11.3: Protect recovery data with the same controls as the original data, such as encryption or separation.
11.4: Keep an isolated instance of recovery data, offline, in the cloud or off site.
11.5: Test backup recovery for a sampling of in-scope enterprise assets.
12.1: Keep network infrastructure current; latest stable software or supported network-as-a-service offerings are example approaches.
Check software versions at least monthly to verify support.
12.2: Maintain a secure network architecture addressing segmentation, least privilege and availability through design and policy as well as documentation.
12.3: Manage network infrastructure securely, for example through version-controlled configuration and secure administration protocols.
12.4: Maintain architecture diagrams, other network-system documentation, or both.
Review and update documentation at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
12.5: Centralize network authentication, authorization and auditing (AAA).
12.6: Use secure network management and communication protocols, such as 802.1X and WPA2 Enterprise or later.
12.7: Require user authentication to enterprise-managed VPN and authentication services before enterprise resources are accessed from end-user devices.
12.8: Use dedicated computing resources for administrative tasks, separated physically or logically from other work, segmented from the primary network and without internet access.
13.1: Centralize security alerts for correlation and analysis. A SIEM with vendor correlation alerts or log analytics with security-relevant correlation alerts can support this.
13.2: Deploy host-based intrusion detection on enterprise assets where appropriate and/or supported.
13.3: Deploy network intrusion detection where appropriate.
13.4: Filter traffic between network segments where appropriate.
13.5: Manage access control for assets that connect remotely, based on up-to-date anti-malware, configuration and patch status.
13.6: Collect network-device traffic flow logs, network traffic, or both for review and alerting.
13.7: Deploy host-based intrusion prevention on enterprise assets where appropriate and/or supported, for example an EDR client or host IPS agent.
13.8: Deploy network intrusion prevention where appropriate.
13.9: Use port-level access control such as 802.1X with certificates or user authentication.
13.10: Filter traffic at the application layer, for example with a filtering proxy or application firewall.
14.1: Maintain an awareness program that teaches the workforce to handle enterprise assets and data securely.
Train at hire and at least annually. Review and update content annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
14.2: Train the workforce to recognize social engineering such as phishing, business email compromise and tailgating.
14.3: Train the workforce on authentication best practices such as MFA, password composition and credential management.
14.4: Train the workforce in identifying, storing, transferring, archiving and destroying sensitive data, including clear-screen/desk practices and secure storage of assets and information.
14.5: Train the workforce on causes of unintentional data exposure, such as misdelivery or lost devices.
14.6: Train the workforce to recognize a potential incident and report it.
14.7: Train the workforce to check and report outdated patches or failed automated processes/tools, including notification to IT when automation fails.
14.8: Train the workforce about insecure networks and data transmission. Where remote workers exist, include secure home-network configuration guidance.
14.9: Run role-specific security awareness and skills training, for example for administrators and developers.
15.1: Keep an inventory of service providers with classification and an enterprise contact for each.
Review and update the inventory at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
15.2: Have a service provider management policy covering classification, inventory, assessment, monitoring and decommissioning.
Review and update the policy at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
15.3: Classify service providers by characteristics such as data sensitivity, volume and availability needs.
Review and update the classifications at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
15.4: Put security requirements in service-provider contracts consistent with the enterprise's provider-management policy; notification, encryption and disposal terms are examples.
Review contracts at least annually for missing security requirements.
15.5: Assess providers under the provider-management policy, varying scope by classification and using suitably rigorous reports, questionnaires or other methods.
Reassess at least annually, or with new and renewed contracts.
15.6: Monitor service providers according to the management policy, such as reassessment and release-note monitoring.
15.7: Decommission service providers securely: deactivate accounts, end data flows and dispose of enterprise data.
16.1: Document the secure-development process, covering design, coding, developer training, vulnerability handling, third-party code security and application testing.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
16.2: Document vulnerability reporting, including external reports, handling ownership, intake, assignment, remediation and testing. Track severity and timing metrics for identification, analysis and remediation; external developers should make reporting expectations clear.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
16.3: Perform root cause analysis on security vulnerabilities.
16.4: Inventory current and planned third-party development components and their risks.
Evaluate the list at least monthly for changes or updates and verify continued component support.
16.5: Keep third-party components current and trusted. Prefer proven secure frameworks/libraries when possible; acquire from trusted sources or assess vulnerabilities before use.
16.6: Maintain application-vulnerability severity ratings and prioritization, including minimum security-acceptability criteria for releasing code or applications.
Review and update the system and process at least annually.
16.7: Apply standard hardening templates to application infrastructure, including servers, databases, web servers and cloud/PaaS/SaaS components. In-house software must not weaken hardening.
16.8: Keep production and non-production systems separate.
16.9: Train developers in application security concepts and secure coding.
16.10: Use secure architecture principles such as least privilege, validating every user operation and input, and reducing unnecessary services, exposed ports and default accounts.
16.11: Use vetted security modules/services for functions such as identity, encryption and auditing. Encryption algorithms must be standardized, currently accepted and extensively reviewed.
16.12: Use static and dynamic analysis tools in the application lifecycle.
16.13: Conduct application penetration testing. Authenticated testing is especially useful for finding business-logic weaknesses in critical applications.
16.14: Conduct threat modeling to find and address design flaws before code is written.
17.1: Name a primary incident-handling lead and at least one backup to coordinate and document response/recovery. When using an external provider, retain a named internal overseer.
Review and update the roles and oversight at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
17.2: Keep contact details for parties that need to be told about incidents, such as staff, providers, insurers and authorities.
17.3: Document workforce incident reporting: timeframes, recipients, reporting mechanism and minimum information. Make the process available to all workforce members.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
17.4: Have a documented incident response process with roles, compliance requirements and a communication plan.
Review and update the process at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
17.5: Assign incident-response responsibilities across legal, IT, security, facilities, public relations, HR, responders and analysts.
Review and update the roles and responsibilities at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
17.6: Define primary and backup channels for incident communication/reporting, accounting for channels such as email being disrupted by the incident.
Review and update the communication mechanisms at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
17.7: Run incident-response exercises for key personnel, testing communication channels, decisions and workflows.
17.8: Run post-incident reviews to prevent recurrence by finding lessons learned and follow-up actions.
17.9: Set and maintain security incident thresholds, at minimum distinguishing an incident from an event.
Review and update the thresholds at least annually and after relevant significant enterprise changes.
18.1: Maintain a penetration-testing program suited to enterprise size, complexity, industry and maturity. Define scope, frequency, limitations, contacts, finding-remediation routing and retrospective expectations.
18.2: Have a qualified party conduct external penetration tests under the program, including enterprise and environmental reconnaissance for exploitable information.
18.3: Remediate penetration-test findings through the documented vulnerability-remediation process, setting effort and timelines by impact and priority.
18.4: Validate security measures after each penetration test and adjust rulesets and capabilities as needed.
18.5: Perform periodic internal penetration tests based on program requirements.
